summary: The persistence layer. It builds the SQLAlchemy engine and session factory from `settings.database_url` (SQLite by default, tuned with WAL mode and foreign-key enforcement), declares the five tables as typed ORM models (`User`, `Device`, `Incident`, `Event`, `RiskSignal`), and provides schema create/reset helpers plus `get_session`, the per-request session every route receives through `routes/deps.py`. The pipeline, correlation, queries, seeder and live-traffic code all read and write through these models.

notes.text: Docstring title. SQLAlchemy is an ORM (object-relational mapper): it maps Python classes to database tables so the code works with objects instead of hand-written SQL, and version 2.0 adds fully typed models.

SQLite is the default because it needs no server: the whole database is one file under `data/`. Any other SQLAlchemy URL can be supplied through `IIP_DB_URL`, and the SQLite-only tweaks below switch themselves off in that case.

Postponed annotations matter here: hints such as `Mapped[datetime]` are stored as strings, and SQLAlchemy resolves them by name when each model class is built. That is why `datetime` and `Any` below are ordinary runtime imports.
`Iterator` annotates a generator function; `get_session` at the bottom yields one `Session`.
`datetime` types the timestamp columns, `Any` the values inside free-form JSON dictionaries.

Core SQLAlchemy pieces: column types (`JSON`, `DateTime`, length-limited `String`, unlimited `Text`), the `ForeignKey` and `Index` constraints, `create_engine` to connect, and `event` to hook into connection life-cycle events.

ORM pieces in the 2.0 style: `DeclarativeBase` is the parent class for models, `Mapped[...]` annotates a typed column attribute, `mapped_column()` adds column options, `Session` is a unit of work (one conversation with the database), and `sessionmaker` builds pre-configured sessions.
Pulls the `data/` folder path and the shared `settings` from `config.py`.
Records once whether the configured URL is a SQLite one (SQLite URLs start with `sqlite`), because several options below only apply to SQLite.
SQLite creates the database file on first connect but not a missing folder, so `data/` is created up front; `exist_ok=True` makes this a no-op when the folder already exists.

Creates the **engine**, SQLAlchemy's connection factory and pool. `check_same_thread=False` disables a check in Python's `sqlite3` driver that forbids using a connection from any thread except the one that opened it; FastAPI runs ordinary (non-async) endpoints in a thread pool and the live-traffic generator writes from worker threads, so connections must move between threads, and other databases reject the option, hence the conditional.

`SessionLocal` is the session factory: each `SessionLocal()` call returns a new `Session` bound to the engine. `expire_on_commit=False` keeps loaded attribute values usable after `commit()`, so a route can serialize an event right after the pipeline commits it without SQLAlchemy reloading the object with another query.

`@event.listens_for(engine, "connect")` registers `_configure_sqlite` to run each time the pool opens a brand-new low-level connection. It receives the raw DB-API connection (the `sqlite3` object) and a pool record it does not need, hence the `_record` name.
The docstring states the two goals, each implemented by one PRAGMA below (a PRAGMA is a SQLite-specific settings command).
Only for SQLite: opens a raw cursor so these database-specific commands can be sent directly.

Turns on write-ahead logging (WAL): new changes go to a separate `-wal` file, so readers keep seeing the last committed data while a writer works, whereas in SQLite's default rollback-journal mode readers and a committing writer block each other. This is what lets the live-traffic writer and the dashboard readers work side by side, and it is why `data/` holds `iip.db-wal` and `iip.db-shm` files next to `iip.db`.

SQLite ignores `FOREIGN KEY` constraints unless this PRAGMA is on, and it applies only to the current connection, which is why it runs on every connect. With it, an event pointing at a non-existent user is rejected instead of being stored as an orphan.
Closes the cursor; the connection itself stays open in the pool.

`Base` is the declarative base every model inherits from. It owns `Base.metadata`, the registry of all table definitions that `init_db()` and `reset_db()` use; the body is just `pass` because no shared behaviour is needed.
`User` maps to the `users` table (`__tablename__` sets the SQL name): one row per synthetic NovaBank customer, created by `seed.py`.

Primary key: a short string such as `USR-1001` rather than an auto-number. `Mapped[str]` gives the Python type, and since it is not optional the column is `NOT NULL`; `String(16)` sets the SQL length.

`name` is the display name, `home_location` the canonical city label (e.g. `Dubai, UAE`) that the "Unusual location" rule compares against, and `segment` the customer tier (Retail, Premier or Business in the seed data).
`Device` maps to `devices`: every device ID seen for a user and whether it is trusted.
Primary key: a device ID such as `DEV-2000`.

`ForeignKey("users.id")` links each device to its owner; the column even copies its type (`VARCHAR(16)`) from `users.id`, so no `String` is needed. `index=True` speeds up the frequent "devices of this user" lookups, e.g. when the simulator picks a trusted device.
`Mapped[bool]` becomes a boolean column, and `default=False` is filled in on insert when no value is given. The pipeline registers unseen devices as untrusted; only the seeder creates trusted ones.
`Incident` maps to `incidents`: one investigation grouping a user's related risky events, created and maintained by `correlation.py`.
`Mapped[int]` plus `primary_key=True` gives an auto-incrementing integer key that the database assigns on insert. The API displays it as `INC-0001` (`queries.incident_ref`).
The affected user, indexed because correlation looks up the user's unresolved incident for every sufficiently risky event.
Triage state (`OPEN`, `INVESTIGATING` or `RESOLVED`), starting as `OPEN`; indexed because incident lists and dashboard counts filter by it.
`severity` (a level such as `HIGH`) and `risk_score` (0-100) are summaries recomputed by `correlation.refresh_incident`: the highest score among the incident's events, and that score's level.

Signal names stored as a JSON array in one column. `default=list` passes the `list` function itself, so every new row gets its own fresh empty list instead of sharing one mutable object; and because SQLAlchemy does not notice in-place edits inside a JSON value, `refresh_incident` always assigns a brand-new list.
The recommended action for the incident's severity, copied from `rules.ACTIONS`.

When the incident opened and when it last saw activity, both naive UTC (see `clock.py`). `updated` is indexed because incidents are listed most-recent-first and correlation only reuses an incident active within the last 30 minutes.
`Event` maps to `events`, the central fact table: one row per ingested identity or risk event, together with its scoring results.

`__table_args__` adds table-level options; here a composite index on `(user_id, timestamp)` serves the most common query shape, "this user's events in a time window, newest first", used by the pipeline's history lookups and the user views. Because `user_id` is the index's leading column, plain per-user filters use it too, so `user_id` needs no separate index.
Integer primary key, displayed to clients as `EVT-00042`.
Owner of the event, enforced as a foreign key to `users`.
`event_type` (login, transaction, resource_access, password_reset) and `timestamp` are both indexed: the event list filters by type, and almost every query sorts or windows by time.
`String(45)` fits the longest textual form of an IPv6 address, so both IPv4 and IPv6 fit. Indexed for the password-spray check, which counts failures from one IP across accounts.
`location` holds the canonical city label produced by `geo.canonical`; `device_id` is a plain string column (not a foreign key) recording the device the client reported.
`Mapped[bool]` with no `mapped_column()` at all: in SQLAlchemy 2.0 the annotation alone defines a `NOT NULL` boolean column. It records whether the device was new to this user when the event arrived.
`failed_attempts` is the failure count the client reported (default 0), and `ip_reputation` is `clean`, `suspicious` or `malicious`.

Optional fields: the `| None` in `float | None` and `str | None` makes the columns nullable, and `transaction_amount` needs no `mapped_column()` at all. `transaction_amount` feeds the transaction rules and `resource_accessed` the privileged-access rule; both are normally empty for other event types.
Whether the action succeeded: `success` or `failure`.

The engine's verdict: `risk_score` (0-100, another annotation-only column) and `risk_level` (LOW to CRITICAL). `risk_level` is indexed for the event list's risk filter and the dashboard's per-level counts.

Explanation data stored as JSON: `signals` lists the raised signal names (heaviest first), `contributions` holds each signal's weight, detail text and MITRE link for the waterfall chart, and `context` keeps enrichment such as the travel calculation drawn on the world map. `default=list` and `default=dict` give each row its own fresh empty value.
`action` is the recommended response for the level and `explanation` the plain-English summary from `rules.assess`; `Text` has no length limit.
The incident this event was correlated into. `int | None` makes it nullable since most events never join one, and it is indexed because incident timelines load their events by this column.

`RiskSignal` maps to a deliberately narrow table with one row per raised signal, as the docstring says. Counting signals inside JSON arrays would need database-specific JSON functions, whereas this table lets the dashboard's top-signals chart use a plain `GROUP BY name`.
SQL table name `risk_signals`.
Integer key plus `event_id`, the indexed foreign key linking each row to the event that raised it.

The signal's `name` (indexed, because the dashboard groups by it) and its `weight` copied at the moment it was raised; the dashboard filters `weight > 0` to leave out "Trusted device". `pipeline.process_event` writes these rows right after storing each event.

`init_db()` creates any tables that do not exist yet and leaves existing tables and their data untouched; `app.py` calls it at start-up. There are no migrations, so after changing a model the database has to be reset.
`reset_db()` drops every table and recreates them empty. It backs `python -m iip --reset` and the Simulation Center's reset endpoint, both of which re-seed straight afterwards.

`get_session` is a **FastAPI dependency**, a function FastAPI calls to supply a parameter for each request. `routes/deps.py` wraps it as the `DB` type, so any endpoint declaring `db: DB` receives its own fresh session.

Because the function uses `yield`, FastAPI runs it up to the `yield`, injects the session into the endpoint, and resumes it once the request has been handled. The `with` block then closes the session and returns its connection to the pool, even if the endpoint raised an error.
